beats.text: Near Kingston, Oklahoma, there's a town at the bottom of a lake.
beats.label: NEAR KINGSTON, OKLAHOMA

beats.text: The town was Woodville. It began in 1881 as Harney, in the Chickasaw Nation, and was renamed Woodville in 1888.
beats.label: POST OFFICE, 1881

beats.text: Then came the Denison Dam on the Red River. Work began in 1939. Woodville stood where the lake would be.
beats.label: THE DENISON DAM
beats.credit: Texas Water Development Board · AI-generated picture

beats.text: The people had to go. Some moved to a new town, called New Woodville.
beats.label: NEW WOODVILLE

beats.text: The dam was finished in 1944. Lake Texoma rose, and old Woodville went under.
beats.credit: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers · AI-generated picture

beats.text: Then, in the drought of 2011, the water dropped. And the foundations of Woodville came back into the light.
beats.label: THE DROUGHT OF 2011

beats.text: If the lake ever shows you the old town, look, but don't take anything. Removing artifacts from federal land is against the law.
beats.label: LOOK, DON'T TAKE
beats.credit: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, via The Madill Record · AI-generated picture

beats.text: Comment your town, and it could be next.

end_card.pill: Lake Texoma: look, but taking artifacts is illegal
